content.title: About
content.content: Underripe plantains are large, greenish fruits of the banana tree (Musa spp.) that are commonly used in cooking either raw or after heat treatment. Unlike ripe bananas they have a dense, starchy flesh, a neutral taste and a slightly bitter note. They are fried, boiled, baked or mashed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Plantains are often called “cooking bananas” because they are more starchy and less sweet than dessert bananas.
In many tropical regions plantains are a staple carbohydrate source comparable to rice or corn.
Raw underripe plantains contain resistant starch that acts as a prebiotic and supports gut health.
In Caribbean cuisine they are known as “tostones” after being fried twice.
Plantains can be grown as perennials, with each stem producing several bunches of fruit each season.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Underripe plantains provide a high amount of starch that releases energy slowly, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: A medium plantain supplies about 15 % of the daily vitamin C requirement, supporting immunity and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: High in potassium
items.content: Potassium aids fluid balance and blood‑pressure regulation; plantains contain more potassium than many other fruits.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Resistant starch and dietary fiber promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Plantains contain virtually no fat, making them a good base for low‑calorie meals.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: Underripe plantains may contain small amounts of solanine, a glycoalkaloid that is toxic in large doses. Cooking destroys it.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to banana family plants, experiencing skin rash or swelling.

items.title: High glycemic index after cooking
items.content: Frying or boiling converts starch to more rapidly digestible forms, which can raise blood sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Underripe plantains are usually peeled, sliced and fried (plantain chips or tostones), boiled in stews, baked, or mashed. They can be cut into thin rounds and crisp‑fried, added to salads, or served as a side dish with meat or fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store underripe plantains in a cool, dry place at 13‑15 °C. Lower temperatures may cause chilling injury, while higher temperatures accelerate ripening. For short‑term storage keep them in the refrigerator in a plastic bag, but use within 5 days.
